origin: The post restates the paper's findings closely, with two checkable misstatements: The paper's "increased drought severity by an average of 40%" becomes "responsible for about 40% of the increase in drought severity". Those are different quantities. The paper compares drought area in 2018 to 2022 with the 1981 to 2017 average ("expanded by 74% on average compared with 1981–2017"). The post says drought area "rose by 74%" from 2018 to 2022, which reads as a rise within that period. Expected honest rating: 60 to 80 (drafter's range, set before the second misstatement was identified; the start may sit lower).

evidence_down.evidence_note: Real. Nature, "Retraction Note: Warming accelerates global drought severity", published 2026-09-02, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11027-z. Verbatim: "The authors have retracted this article after being notified of errors in the paper and independently identifying further issues. First, area-weighted grid cells were not used when calculating study-wide averages, an error that affected numerical values in the main text [...]" and "given the scope of the necessary corrections and the need for additional revision and peer review, the authors have decided to retract the paper and to resubmit a fully revised and corrected version for peer review. All authors agree with the retraction." Retraction Watch (2026-09-02, https://retractionwatch.com/2026/09/02/oxford-researchers-retract-nature-paper-on-atmospheric-thirst-for-calculation-errors/) quotes the lead author saying the corrected number "will be slightly lower" and that "none of the paper's conclusions are affected".
pushes: New information that adds to the fact sheet: on September 2, 2026, Nature retracted the study the article reports. The retraction notice says the authors were notified of errors and found further issues: study-wide averages were computed without area-weighting grid cells, which changed numerical values in the main text; one figure used an older evaporation dataset; and a timestepping error affected regional drought-area results. The authors plan to resubmit a corrected version. The lead author said the corrected figure will be slightly lower and that the conclusion that warming likely worsened drought severity still holds. Does that change your rating?
Makes sense. What is your final number?
